title: Minimize Malware Spread II
description:
# Minimize Malware Spread II

You are given an undirected network of `n` nodes as an `n x n` adjacency matrix `graph`. The value `graph[i][j] == 1` means nodes `i` and `j` are directly connected.

Some nodes in `initial` are infected by malware. Malware spreads through connected edges: if either endpoint of an edge is infected, the other endpoint eventually becomes infected. The spread continues until no more nodes can be infected.

You may choose exactly one node from `initial` and remove that node from the graph completely, including all of its incident edges. Return the node whose removal minimizes the final number of infected nodes. If several choices produce the same minimum, return the smallest node index.

This differs from the first Malware Spread problem: here the chosen node and its edges disappear from the graph, rather than only being removed from the initial infected list.

## Example 1

**Input:** graph = [[1,1,0],[1,1,0],[0,0,1]], initial = [0,1]
**Output:** 0
**Explanation:** Removing either 0 or 1 leaves only one infected node, so the tie is resolved by the smaller index 0.

## Example 2

**Input:** graph = [[1,1,0],[1,1,1],[0,1,1]], initial = [0,1]
**Output:** 1
**Explanation:** Removing node 1 also cuts its bridge to node 2, so fewer nodes are infected.

## Example 3

**Input:** graph = [[1,1,0,0],[1,1,1,0],[0,1,1,1],[0,0,1,1]], initial = [0,1]
**Output:** 1

## Constraints

* `n == graph.length == graph[i].length`
* `2 <= n <= 300`
* `graph[i][j]` is `0` or `1`
* `graph[i][i] == 1`
* `graph[i][j] == graph[j][i]`
* `1 <= initial.length < n`
* All values in `initial` are unique.

solutions.name: BFS Simulation per Removed Node
solutions.description:
## Approach
Sort `initial` so tie handling is natural. For each candidate node, skip it completely and run BFS from every other initially infected node through the remaining graph. Count how many nodes become infected.

## Key Insight
Because the chosen node is removed together with its edges, every traversal must ignore that node both as a source and as a neighbor. Brute-force simulation is slower, but it directly matches the statement and is a reliable baseline.

## Complexity Analysis
Let `m = initial.length`. Each candidate simulation scans an adjacency matrix during BFS, costing `O(n^2)`; trying all candidates costs `O(m * n^2)` time and `O(n)` space.

solutions.name: DFS Simulation per Removed Node
solutions.description:
## Approach
Try each initially infected node as the removed node. For that candidate, launch DFS from all remaining initially infected nodes and mark every reachable node except the removed one.

## Key Insight
DFS and BFS compute the same reachable infected set. Writing the simulation recursively makes the removed-node guard explicit at the entrance to every traversal step.

## Complexity Analysis
For each candidate, DFS over an adjacency matrix can inspect `O(n^2)` entries. Across `m` candidates the time is `O(m * n^2)`, with `O(n)` visited storage and recursion depth.

solutions.name: Union-Find After Candidate Removal
solutions.description:
## Approach
For each candidate removal, rebuild connected components on all nodes except the removed node. The final infected nodes are exactly the nodes in components containing one of the remaining initially infected nodes.

## Key Insight
After deleting a candidate and its edges, infection fills whole connected components. Counting infected components avoids running a graph traversal from every source for that candidate.

## Complexity Analysis
Rebuilding union-find for each of the `m` candidates scans the matrix, so the time is `O(m * n^2)`. Parent, size, and infected-root arrays use `O(n)` space.

solutions.name: Clean Component Ownership by BFS Labels
solutions.description:
## Approach
Temporarily remove every initially infected node, then label connected components made only of clean nodes. A clean component can be saved by removing source `x` only if it is adjacent to exactly one initially infected source, and that source is `x`.

## Key Insight
Nodes already infected in `initial` except the removed one are unavoidable. The only decision-dependent part is how many clean nodes become protected, so maximizing saved clean component sizes is equivalent to minimizing final infection.

## Complexity Analysis
The component labeling and ownership scans both use the adjacency matrix, giving `O(n^2)` time and `O(n)` auxiliary space.

solutions.name: Clean Component Ownership with Union-Find
solutions.description:
## Approach
Use union-find once on only the clean nodes, ignoring all initially infected nodes. For each infected source, collect the clean component roots it touches; a component contributes to a source only if no other source touches it.

## Key Insight
This is the same ownership idea as component labeling, but the component construction is expressed as disjoint-set unions. It avoids rebuilding the graph for each candidate while still respecting complete removal of one infected source.

## Complexity Analysis
Unioning clean edges and scanning infected-to-clean adjacency both cost `O(n^2)` on the matrix. The disjoint-set arrays and ownership arrays require `O(n)` space.
